english_classification.chapter_note: Chapter 100 explicitly cites the Persian Magian tradition ('the laws of the Magi') as the source of the fourteen-headed dragon teaching. The core substrate is concentrated in paragraphs 4-6, which systematically map: 14 dragon heads → 7 upper sense organs + 7 lower body parts; 5 dens → tongue, lungs, heart, spleen, blood. The key identification (dragon = 'the thought of the body') appears in paragraph 7 embedded in exhortation. The teaching is framed by editorial dialogue (P1-2) and closed by a beatitude (P9). Despite the chapter's modest length, the body-correspondence substrate is remarkably clean and well-preserved. The explicit Persian provenance is significant — the teaching is presented as a spiritual reinterpretation of a Magian cosmological image, suggesting the substrate preserves an older Persian body-cosmos correspondence tradition.
